https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2026/07.text: Menu Search Latest Profile English Contact | About | International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Menu Search International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Latest Profile Fourth International Socialist Equality Party IYSSE About the WSWS Contact Donate More than 375,000 people have been driven from their homes and holiday accommodation in France and Spain as the wildfires produced by Europe’s third heatwave of the summer sweep across a continent enduring what is the worst heatwave season ever recorded. The figure is climbing inexorably towards 400,000 with the city council of French city Bordeaux considering a “total evacuation if needed”. Smoke and flames rise as a wildfire advances near La Adrada, Ávila province, Spain, Friday, July 24, 2026 [AP Photo/Manu Fernandez] A heat dome over Europe has driven record temperatures in many countries. At the late-June peak, temperatures ran 14-18°C above normal across much of the continent. The heat has not relented since. As the latest fires took hold a temperature of 48.4 °C was recorded at Casteltermini in Sicily on July 18—the highest recorded temperature in Europe so far during this heatwave. On Thursday temperatures reached 44 °C across southeastern interior Spain and the Guadalquivir Valley. According to interior minister Laurent Nuñez, France saw what was “probably” the biggest peacetime civilian evacuation it has ever seen. Over the weekend authorities ordered the total clearance, by land and sea, of the Gironde region of the south west—one of the country’s main holiday destinations—and the port city of Bordeaux with a metropolitan population of 850,000 began drawing up plans for its own evacuation. By Sunday more than 220,000 people had been evacuated from the path of the main forest fire in southwest France as almost 98,000 hectares burned nationally, a record. The fire that began near Saumos in the Gironde on Wednesday generated its own weather, with Sébastien Berge, head of the Gironde firefighters’ union, saying his members were “overwhelmed” by a fire front stretching more than 20km. On Sunday, Nuñez said the fires “remained extremely violent, unpredictable” as they edged towards Bordeaux. Around 44,000 fled the Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast, its only access road threatened by the flames, with boats ferrying hundreds off the piers. At Biscarrosse to the south, evacuees included a children’s summer camp and a care home for the elderly. Jean Mazodier, 86, evacuated from his forest home at dawn, told Le Monde : “Everything’s burned. It’s like losing a child.” By the weekend the fire had turned towards Bordeaux, with evacuation orders issued across a widening span of suburbs along with the city’s airport, as around 55,000 people were cleared from villages on the city’s approaches overnight. Mayor Thomas Cazenave said the fire was “at the gates of the metropolitan area” and the city council was studying scenarios up to a total evacuation. Sixty-eight firefighters had been injured tackling the fires in the south-west. More than 1,500 French soldiers and 1,700 additional security personnel have been deployed, with an A400M military transport plane joining water bombers. Sunday’s finale of the Tour de France in Paris was shortened after security forces were redeployed. President Emmanuel Macron activated the European Union’s civil protection mechanism, securing aircraft and personnel from Croatia, Portugal, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, with Germany sending helicopters and rescue teams. That the head of state of one of the world’s largest economies must appeal across the continent for aircraft in an emergency forecast for months is an admission that no capitalist government across Europe maintains the means to protect its population. Evacuees are housed at the Bordeaux Exhibition Centre in Bordeaux, France, after having to leave their homes outside town due to the raging wildfires, Sunday, July 26, 2026 [AP Photo/Caroline Blumberg] In Spain, a national emergency was declared Thursday over wildfires for the first time ever, with more than 90,000 people told to flee. Such a declaration has been made only once before, during the nationwide blackout of April 2025 . On Saturday evening the interior ministry said a man had been found dead in his car in a ravine near Valencia. Three firefighters have lost their lives; one in Italy and two in France. Two wind-driven fires in the Ávila and Madrid provinces merged into a single blaze, moving towards the municipalities of Robledo de Chavela and Fresnedillas de la Oliva, around 50km west of the capital. In response, operational command transferred to the military’s emergency unit. Nearly 30,000 people were evacuated across the Madrid region, with further evacuations near Toledo and in Castellón in the east. Madrid’s regional emergency chief, Carlos Novillo, admitted that the fire was “at its peak and currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain”. Regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso called it “the worst wildfire in our region’s history.” El Mundo reported some 24,000 hectares burned in the Madrid region and 21,000 in Ávila. Spain, too, requested aircraft through the EU mechanism. In Italy, more than 40,000 hectares have burned nationally since the start of the year, an 81 percent increase on the recent average. Wildfires had been raging for days across Sicily, where temperatures topped 40C and gusts of hot wind fanned the flames. In midweek, around 6,000 firefighters, forest guards and civil protection officials, with the help of water-bombing aircraft, were deployed on the island to at least 50 fires the regional head Renato Schifani said. The fires spread this weekend from Sicily to the mainland. On Sunday a large blaze on the Gargano promontory in Puglia reached the coast, with more than a thousand tourists evacuated from beaches by boat. In Sicily, civil protection again raised its highest fire alert for the provinces of Palermo and Trapani. In Greece, firefighters responded to 50 rural and forest fires across multiple regions in 24 hours. To Vima reported on Thursday that most were brought under control in their initial stages by ground crews and aerial units. The largest operations were at Zoniana, in the regional unit of Rethymno on Crete; Afidnes in Attica; Ano Kerasovo near Agrinio; Kalligata on the island of Kefalonia; Imero Pefko in Pikermi; and Perachora near Loutraki. Attica (containing the capital Athens), Evia and Rhodes were placed under a red-code alert for very high fire risk. The engulfing of much of southern Europe by forest fires, worse than any before, is the result of world governments’ failure to do what is needed to restrict carbon emissions and global heating, compounded by decades of defunded forestry and civil protection. It is not just in the hotter climates that fires have broken out, but also in the north from the UK to Norway. Britain, the sixth largest economy in the world, possesses no aerial firefighting capability of any kind. In the Cairngorms National Park in Scotland, a blaze burning since July 15 has required more than 500 firefighters to tackle it. Scottish National Party First Minister John Swinney has asked Andy Burnham’s UK Labour “government for military assistance in aerial support... and we await a response.” North Wales and the Upper Severn are the first parts of Britain to declare a drought, having received just 3 percent of its average July rainfall, with a fourth heatwave forecast for the coming week. An analysis published this week by the World Weather Attribution consortium found the evaporative conditions drying out the continent were made 80 times more likely by global heating in western Europe and 40 times more likely in the east. On Friday, World Health Organization Europe head Hans Henri P. Kluge warned, “As climate change drives a warming world, we need to prepare for more frequent and intense wildfires.” Since 2022, the number of wildfires has risen by 57 percent across the WHO European Region. Portugal and Spain have suffered a 100 percent increase in wildfires this year compared with 2025. According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), last year alone, around 2.2 million hectares burned, while 254,388 hectares had already been destroyed by July 22 this year. In the days since, the destruction has significantly worsened. France, with Paris playing a central role, is the most visited country in the world receiving more than 100 million annual foreign visitors. The response of the French state to the ongoing social catastrophe was that nothing should impact the bottom line, with Foreign Office minister Éléonore Caroit telling the BBC Saturday that tourists should not cancel their holidays. “I’m in Paris and nothing is happening [!], and most other regions are OK,” she said. This was less than two weeks after fire had torn through some 2,000 hectares of the Fontainebleau forest just south-east of Paris, forcing the evacuation of 1,000 people and compelling water-bombers to scoop from the Seine to protect the capital region for the first time in its history. As the WSWS reported on July 14, European mortality monitoring body EuroMOMO had by then attributed roughly 10,600 deaths to this summer’s heat, with an analysis by Politico identifying 14,000 excess deaths in six countries—Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain and the UK—during the June heatwave alone. This excluded deaths in other heavily impacted countries such as Italy, Portugal and Greece. The World Health Organisation estimates extreme heat has killed some 200,000 people in Europe in four years, deaths it said were for the most part “entirely preventable.” They are not prevented because society’s resources, controlled by the super-rich capitalist class and governments which serve their interests, have been allocated elsewhere. The same governments now appealing to one another for water bombers against the flames are pouring hundreds of billions into rearmament. Six of Europe’s leading oil companies made $21.7 billion in profits in the first quarter of this year, 43 percent up on 2025. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Publishing Ukrainian publishers call for support after Russian attacks destroy 10m books The country risks ‘the collapse of the entire book ecosystem’ following destruction of warehouses in July and August, say Ukrainian publishers Emma Loffhagen Thu 20 Aug 2026 11.37 EDT Last modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Ukrainian Book Institute has called on the international publishing community to support Ukrainian publishers after Russian attacks in July and early August destroyed about 10m books and a significant share of the country’s book production capacity. The institute said the attacks on publishing, printing and warehouse infrastructure had left some companies at risk of financial collapse. A major attack on 1 August hit warehouses belonging to the RNK-Ranok publishing group in Kharkiv, destroying approximately 8m books, following July attacks in Kyiv which led to the loss of more than 1.5m books. In all, the recent attacks have led to the destruction of approximately 30% of the volume of books produced annually in Ukraine . The RNK-Ranok logistics centre, which stores books for the company’s many imprints, is also the distribution centre for the national bookselling chain KnyhoLand, which runs 51 shops and several websites. Along with the estimated 8m books lost, a further 600,000 school textbooks were destroyed. The total loss has been preliminarily estimated at almost 1bn hryvnias (£16.5m). “At this stage, we face the risk of the collapse of the entire book ecosystem,” said Oleksandra Koval, director of the Ukrainian Book Institute. The institute is asking for donations to support Ukrainian publishers, and is calling on the international publishing community to work with Ukrainian publishers and raise awareness about Russian attacks on Ukrainian culture. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and now occupies about a fifth of Ukrainian territory. On 16 August, a Russian attack on Kyiv led to a fire breaking out at the Pochaina book market, destroying several rows of stalls, books and vendors’ property. The Pochaina market, founded in 1997, was once one of Ukraine’s largest book markets, with hundreds of stalls and books from more than 120 publishers. The institute said the book industry was of “strategic importance” to Ukraine, preserving and promoting Ukrainian culture and giving the country’s voice a platform at home and abroad. The Ukrainian government is developing support programmes for affected publishers and printing companies, including grants to restore equipment and compensation for property damage. But the institute said publishers’ losses could not be fully covered by state assistance. “Against the backdrop of Russia’s ongoing attempts to destroy Ukrainian identity, culture and history, Ukrainian publishing has a special mission,” said Olena Odynoka, deputy director for international cooperation of the Ukrainian Book Institute. “Supporting Ukrainian publishers today is not simply about preserving an industry. It is about defending Ukraine’s right to speak in its own voice and shape its own narrative in the world.” The institute also called for an end to cooperation with Russian publishers and literary agencies, saying that solidarity with Ukrainian publishers was crucial to preserving cultural heritage that Russia was “deliberately trying to destroy”. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/11/war-.text: Iran's pharmaceutical sector is facing shortages of hundreds of medicines, a near-six-fold price hike for basic drugs and collapsing supply chains, as the war with the US enters its seventh month and the effects of sanctions and a naval blockade accumulate.The shortages include roughly 90 medicines classified as essential or life-saving, according to Iranian media.Hadi Ahmadi, spokesperson for the Iranian Pharmacists Association, told domestic media last week that around 400 of the scarce medicines are produced domestically — evidence that local manufacturing has not insulated the sector from disruption, because many domestic producers rely on imported raw materials.Ruhollah Lak Aliabadi, a member of parliament's health commission, told Tabnak news site that access problems for imported inputs were feeding directly into production and distribution failures.Vahideh Mahmoudkhani, head of the health department at Iran's trade centre in Shanghai, told the newspaper Hamshahri that the war had completely shut down some supply routes and made others significantly longer."Even some medicines that have run out are stuck in transit," she said.Tehran, the economic outcastMedicines and humanitarian goods are typically exempt from direct sanctions under international law.But banking restrictions, difficulties transferring foreign currency and blockade-related transport disruption can prevent Iranian companies from purchasing drugs and raw materials abroad regardless of their formal legal status.The US naval blockade of Iranian ports and cargo vessels imposed in April was briefly lifted following the framework agreement before being reinstated after talks collapsed.Washington launched what it called Operation Economic Outcast in late August, designed to further restrict Tehran's access to international financial networks.Mehdi Pirsalehi, head of Iran's Food and Drug Organisation, said on Tuesday that 44 companies in the medicines and medical equipment sector had been targeted in attacks since the war began, with staff killed and wounded.He made the remarks at the opening of a pharmaceutical exhibition in Tehran, while stressing that two companies struck directly by several missiles were present at the event and had resumed production.One of those companies was Tofigh Daru. In late March, Israeli officials announced they had struck it because of what they said was its role in supplying fentanyl to a research body within Iran's defence ministry.Tofigh Daru rejected the allegation, saying it produced only fentanyl citrate in limited quantities and exclusively for authorised medical uses including surgical anaesthesia.Prices rising beyond reachThe physical shortage of medicines is compounded by price rises that are pricing patients out of treatment.Mehr state news agency has reported that gabapentin — used to treat epilepsy and nerve pain — rose 220% in price over a year.Paracetamol rose 375%, amoxicillin 285% and fluoxetine 100%. Insulin, which diabetic patients require daily, has in some cases reached six times last year's price.The continued depreciation of the rial on the open market is feeding further price increases across the sector.Salman Es'haghi, a member of parliament's health commission, said more than 70% of healthcare costs in Iran are paid directly out of patients' pockets.Ahmad Ariayi Nejad, also on the commission, said the financial pressure was already showing in fewer patients attending clinics and doctors' surgeries.He cited the case of a labourer and tenant who needs two injections a month costing approximately 74 million tomans — a sum that amounts to several months' wages for many Iranians.The consequences are most acute for patients with serious conditions. When treatment for heart disease or cancer is interrupted or delayed for financial reasons, the harm is often irreversible."Some people, because of economic hardship and lack of financial means, abandon their treatment part-way through," Ariayi Nejad said.Tehran has maintained that the pharmaceutical industry continues to operate and that some shortages have eased since the war.

https://www.politico.eu/article/talks-eu.text: MILWAUKEE, Wisconsin — China and the EU “are definitely not there yet” on a prospective trade deal, Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič told POLITICO Thursday, calling months of talks “constructive, but tough.” But the EU’s top trade official also emphasized the political pressure he is under to find that elusive common ground with Beijing. “I feel high political interest and, of course, very high expectations from the leaders all across the European Union,” Šefčovič said in an interview on the sidelines of a meeting of G20 trade ministers in Milwaukee. “I know how politically impatient the European leadership is.” Advertisement Advertisement Šefčovič travels to Beijing Oct. 8 for what he termed a “a super crucial meeting” with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, and said he was optimistic the trip will bear fruit. “You have to believe that you can accomplish something, otherwise you better don’t go.” The commissioner needs to get results he can present at a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Oct. 15-16, and has said previously that Brussels is ready to restrict Chinese access to the EU market should the talks fail. The EU and China have been locked in tense negotiations since June. EU leaders have said they can no longer tolerate the flood of Chinese imports inundating the single market, putting pressure on domestic manufacturers and forcing plant closures and layoffs. “I think our Chinese partners understood that this has direct implication on the future of emblematic European companies — literally thousands of jobs,” Šefčovič reported. “And also the social fabric and social model which was developed in Europe over many, many decades.” The bloc’s ballooning €1-billion-a-day trade deficit with China lies at the heart of the talks. Cutting that deficit would require either reducing imports from China, boosting EU exports, or a mix of the two. Šefčovič said he hopes to bring a “proof of concept” back from Beijing that addresses three main issues: sudden Chinese export surges in key industrial sectors; tangible ways to increase European goods exports to China; and long-term clarity regarding China’s export curbs on raw materials, especially rare earth elements. Advertisement Advertisement While in Milwaukee, Šefčovič met with Chinese Vice-Minister Li Chenggang. The veteran Slovak commissioner said China understands Europe’s worries: “All the issues we suggested are on the table. I’m not saying that we have clear-cut reassurances that we will solve them, but they are on the table.” “Some of these topics have been very difficult to put on the agenda in the past. I believe this reflects the understanding of how politically important this is for both of us.” The bilateral consultations have been divided into four work streams: trade and investment balancing; export controls; intellectual property rights; and reform of the World Trade Organization. One person with knowledge of the negotiations, who asked to remain anonymous due to the sensitivity of the talks, said the Commission was seeking a settlement with China that would involve a mix of bilateral agreements on certain product categories, coupled with unilateral restrictions on others. The Commission will present the outcome of the negotiations to EU leaders at their mid-October meeting in Brussels. The leaders will then decide whether the results are satisfactory. French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday criticized China for unfairly subsidizing its domestic producers and urged the Commission to deploy more safeguards to protect European industry. China has also signaled that it’s ready to fight back. Responding to an as-yet-unpublished Franco-German position paper that is expected to urge an upgrade to the EU’s trade defenses, a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said China would take “firm action” against any moves to restrict goods from entering the European single market.
